verdict.reasoning: The doctor opens with, “You've been saying there's a problem with your hearing, is that right?” and the patient confirms decreased hearing, indicating presentation with a hearing problem.

Patient states decreased hearing in the left ear and duration: “I just feel like I can't really hear as well as I used to…”, and confirms side and time: “Just the left ear, yeah.” and “For about six weeks.”

Patient reports, “I occasionally get like a ringing in my left ear just on the one side… It's kind of on and off. Like some things trigger it as well. So, for example, if I'm watching TV or listening to music or something. Something that will set off the ringing in the ear.”

Patient describes intermittent dizziness: “there's actually been a few times when I felt kind of a bit sick or a bit dizzy as well” and later clarifies, “It's not that kind of dizziness you get with nausea, like not proper room spinning or anything like that, but just a little bit kind of off balance,” which distinguishes it from vertigo.

The doctor asks, “And have you had any pain from the ear at all? Okay.” but the patient’s verbal response is not recorded; only the doctor’s filler “Okay” is present, so an explicit denial of ear pain is not documented.

The doctor asks, “Any discharge coming out of the ear? Okay.” but the patient's actual answer is not transcribed; only the doctor’s “Okay” is shown, so there is no explicit documented denial of ear discharge.
The doctor asks, “Have you been experiencing any fever?” and the patient replies, “Not specifically, apart from the dizziness and sickness I mentioned before,” which functions as a denial of fever.
The doctor asks, “And has your ear been itchy at all?” and the patient responds, “No.” This is an explicit denial of ear itch.
Patient describes a prior episodic issue: “I had something maybe about a year ago, but it only lasted a couple of days. It wasn't anything as long as this,” referring to hearing problems.
On cotton bud use: Doctor asks, “do you use cotton wool buds to try and clean out wax from your ears?” Patient answers, “No. I don't know.” The initial “No” supports that he does not use cotton buds.

The consultation is remote and contains no examination findings; instead, the doctor says, “the first thing that we need to do is we need to get someone to have a look inside your ear,” indicating that no physical exam or diagnostic findings are currently documented.

The doctor discusses possible impacted wax/obstruction: “Simple things might be wax. Someone might have impacted wax blocking the tube going into the eardrum, which can lead to muffled hearing. If that's the case, that that's something that's easily fixable… we need to exclude that first.” This is a possible, not confirmed, cause.

The doctor identifies likely tinnitus and uncertainty of cause: “Does it seem like the ringing that you've got that you've got something called tinnitus… we don't really understand it fully… People can't give you a specific cause for why some patients get tinnitus and some patients don't.”

Patient reports intermittent, mild dizziness without classic vertigo: “there's actually been a few times when I felt kind of a bit sick or a bit dizzy as well” and later, “not proper room spinning or anything like that, but just a little bit kind of off balance,” which is intermittent dizziness without major vertigo or other associated symptoms like chest pain or palpitations (both denied).
The doctor plans a face‑to‑face appointment: “we book you in for a face to face appointment in one of our clinics, it's not an emergency, it can be done within the next four, five days or so.”

The doctor explicitly states evaluation for wax blockage: “one of the GP will just have a quick look down the ear, figure out whether there's a physical blockage… Simple things might be wax… we need to exclude that first and try and deal with that if that's the case.”

The doctor plans to provide a tinnitus leaflet: “I'm going to put paste the link for a leaflet about tinnitus in the notes for this appointment. I'd really appreciate it if you could start reading about it.”

The doctor indicates next steps depend on findings: “And then after that we can. We'll be a step closer to figuring out which way we're going to go… if your ear is clear.” This shows follow‑up/management will be based on examination results.
